notes.meaning: The writer cries out to the Lord in a time of crushing personal and national grief. He asks God to listen closely and allow his desperate plea to reach heaven. Even the most faithful believers face seasons of deep trouble where poured-out prayer is their only comfort.

differ.view: Charles Spurgeon held that this is not truly a penitential psalm because it expresses the grief of a sufferer rather than a confession of sin.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine interpreted this opening prayer as the voice of Christ crying out to the Father during His passion.

notes.meaning: The sufferer begs God not to turn away His face while disaster presses hard. He asks the Lord to lean down, listen patiently, and send help right away. Feeling distant from God's loving presence makes any painful trial far heavier to bear.

The writer compares his brief, troubled days to smoke that quickly vanishes into the sky. His bones feel scorched inside, glowing and dry like a heated hearth. Intense sorrow and affliction have drained away his inner vitality.

His heart feels struck down and dried up like grass cut by a blade under a hot sun. He is so consumed by sorrow that he forgets to eat his daily bread. Deep emotional grief often ruins a person's appetite and drains their physical energy.

Long hours of groaning and weeping have taken a severe toll on the sufferer's body. He has become so thin that his skin clings directly to his bones. Persistent inward grief naturally wears out a person's physical frame.

The writer compares himself to lonely birds that live in dry wastes and ruined places. He feels as isolated and mournful as a pelican or an owl sitting among heaps of rubble. Affliction has separated him from ordinary human companionship and gladness.

Sleepless nights keep the sufferer watching while the rest of the world rests. He feels as solitary as a single small bird perched alone upon a roof. When trials isolate us from others, the Lord remains our faithful watcher.

Cruel enemies insult and mock the sufferer throughout the entire day. They are so furious against him that they use his name as an example when swearing a curse. Mockery from opponents adds sharp pain to an already broken spirit.

The psalmist sits in dust and ashes as a sign of deep mourning, so that ashes get into his food. His frequent weeping falls into his cup, mingling tears with whatever he drinks. His whole life has become thoroughly drenched with sorrow.

The sufferer sees God's righteous discipline behind the downfall of his people. He feels like an object that has been lifted high only to be hurled violently to the ground. The hardest part of any trial is the fearful sense that God is angry.

His life seems like an evening shadow that stretches long just before it is swallowed by the dark. He is withering away like grass cut off from moisture. Without God's intervention, he views himself as a dying man with no future.

The psalm turns away from human weakness to focus entirely on the eternal God. While earthly lives fade and end, the Lord remains seated on His throne forever. His fame and covenant promises will be remembered through all generations.

The writer expresses complete confidence that God will step forward and pity Zion. He believes the set time promised for Jerusalem's restoration has finally arrived. God never forgets His appointed schedule to deliver His troubled people.

God's faithful people still love the broken stones and scattered dust of Jerusalem, even while it lies in ruins. Their affection for the destroyed city shows a deep hunger for God's presence and worship to return. When believers truly care for God's house in its lowest state, blessing is near.

When the Lord restores His people, surrounding nations and their kings will look on with reverent awe. Seeing God's power and faithfulness will cause the Gentiles to honor His holy name. God's mercy to His own church serves as a witness to the entire world.

Rebuilding Zion makes the Lord's majesty and brilliance visible to everyone. Earthly rulers put their splendor on display in magnificent cities, but God reveals His greatest glory by renewing His people. His saving power shines brightest when He raises what was ruined.

The Lord turns His ear toward the cries of poor, stripped, and helpless people. While mighty human kings often ignore beggars, God never looks down on the prayers of the destitute. He listens gladly to those who recognize that they have nothing of their own.

This amazing rescue is written down so future generations will know what God has done. People who do not yet exist will read this record and give heartfelt praise to the Lord. Remembering God's past mercies builds faith in the hearts of our children.

differ.view: John Gill explained that a people created can mean sinners who become new creatures in Christ.
John Calvin explained the phrase as the covenant church brought back from the death of exile as if by a brand new creation.

notes.meaning: The Lord leans down from His holy dwelling in heaven to look over the whole earth. From His exalted throne, His eyes actively search out the struggles of human beings. Nothing that happens to His people escapes His caring gaze.

God looks down specifically to listen to the groaning of prisoners held in captivity. He acts with power to release those who had been marked for death. His mercy reaches into the darkest prisons to shatter chains and save lives.

The released captives return to Zion so they can proclaim the name of the Lord. They gather in Jerusalem to tell of His mercy and sing His praises. God frees His people so their grateful lives will make His goodness known.

The praise of God will expand widely when foreign nations and earthly kingdoms gather to serve Him. This looks forward to the day when Gentiles unite with Israel to worship the one true Lord. True worship breaks through national boundaries to unite all peoples under God.

The writer returns to his personal distress, feeling his strength broken in the middle of his journey. He senses that God has cut his lifespan short before he can see these glorious promises fulfilled. Sickness and trouble often make our earthly journey feel prematurely ended.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine, following the Greek Septuagint wording, understood this verse as the unified Church answering God about her days.

notes.meaning: The psalmist begs God not to take his life halfway through his years. He contrasts his own short life with God's unending existence that runs through all generations. Because God lives forever, mortal people can ask Him for extended life and mercy.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine interpreted this as the Church praying to survive until the end of the world, refuting opponents who claimed she had died out.

notes.meaning: In the distant beginning, God laid the foundations of the solid earth and crafted the skies. The universe did not make itself, but came into being through His creative power. Knowing that the Lord made all things assures us that He has the power to rebuild our lives.

The heavens and the earth will eventually wear out and fade like an old coat. The Lord will easily fold them up and replace them like clothing, while He remains completely unchanged. Everything in creation decays, but the Creator stands forever.

God's nature and character never alter, and His years will never come to an end. He remains entirely the same yesterday, today, and forever. Believers can rest peacefully because their God never changes, ages, or fails.

Because God is eternal, the children of His servants will live safely and securely. Their descendants will stand firm and established in His presence from generation to generation. God's everlasting faithfulness guarantees that His church will never be destroyed.

differ.view: John Calvin held that this promise applies to descendants who continue in the faith of their godly parents, not to every physical child.
John Wesley interpreted this as an assurance that Israel's physical children would enjoy a happy return and settlement in their own land.
